newsitem.title: INDIA: Gandhi's heir wins box of ashes after legal battle.
newsitem.headline: Gandhi's heir wins box of ashes after legal battle.

text.p: Mahatma Gandhi's great grandson won control on Tuesday of a wooden box in a bank vault that he claims contains the ashes of modern India's founding father.

The Supreme Court ordered a government-owned bank in the eastern state of Orissa to yield the box to Tushar Arun Gandhi, who has pledged to scatter the purported ashes of his great grandfather in the mighty Ganges River.
The sealed box, measuring 18 inches by 18 inches by 20 inches (45 cm by 45 cm by 50 cm), was deposited with the State Bank of India in Cuttack town on November 29, 1950.
Gandhi was shot dead by a Hindu fanatic on January 30, 1948, five months after India, spurred by the apostle of non-violence, won independence from Britain.

The box bears the inscription "it contains the ashes of Mahatma Gandhi", the Supreme Court said in a 10-page judgement that responded to a request by Tushar Arun Gandhi to take control of the box, stored in the bank's safe deposit vault.

Earlier this year after a flurry of press reports about the supposed ashes, Gandhi's great grandson ran into a bureaucratic wall when he asked for the box to "complete the last rites as per the Hindu religious practice".
Hindus cremate their dead and throw the ashes into a river. The Ganges is considered the holiest.
The state's chief minister said the tale was "a big hoax", but that he was willing to have the contents chemically tested to see if they were truly Mahatma Gandhi's ashes.
Taking a leaf out of his forefather's book, Tushar Arun Gandhi started a fast, and the Orissa government agreed to give him control. But the State Bank balked and told Gandhi he needed a court order.

The Supreme Court, saying it saw no reason why the box should be viewed with suspicion and that it saw "no harm in directing the disposal of the ashes", ordered a senior Orissa court official to take control of the box.

The court said the official, along with Tushar Arun Gandhi and a State Bank representative, "shall carry the ashes to a mutually agreed upon site on the River Ganges for being disposed of with reverence and dignity behoving the occasion".
It left the choice of date up to the court official, the bank and Gandhi's great grandson.
